description: WP5 impact-assessment reference data (D5.2 v5): Macaronesia Table 21 cross-scenario assessment; Arctic Tables 2-7 (revenue by scenario) and Table 8 (political feasibility). Read-only reference cells that users copy into an editable assessment. Tuscan has no scenarios in D5.2 (valuation chapter only).
verification: Cell text is a de-hyphenated transcription of one table column. Table 21 columns are interleaved in the pdftotext -layout extract, so each value carries verify_phrases copied from a single extract line inside its source_lines; tests match them against the extract and against the transcription. Figures carry their published display string, which tests find in the table's line range.

macaronesia.scenario_note: S1-S4 are governance escalation pathways (D5.2 §5.4, L4533-4535); ambition_rank follows that order.

scenarios.confidence_text: High, based on observed current conditions and well-documented governance arrangements
Medium–High, effects are incremental and reasonably predictable, but uptake can vary
Medium, positive impacts are plausible, but depend on governance design and compliance
Low–Medium, outcomes depend heavily on political commitment, funding continuity & benefit-sharing mechanisms and sectoral responses

cells.text: No additional ecological impact beyond existing MPAs, migratory species remain exposed between MPAs, pressures from fisheries, shipping, and tourism continue to be managed in isolation
High short-term efficiency as there are no additional constraints for companies, long-term inefficiencies continue/may arise from unmanaged ecological impacts
Uneven outcomes persist between regions and user groups; e.g. small-scale fisheries receive fewer benefits than larger operators and transit shipping
High, as no changes are required for fisheries, shipping operators, or tourism businesses
High feasibility (no added cost), relies entirely on existing budgets and instruments
Minor ecological improvements through voluntary alignment, e.g. shared guidelines for fisheries or tourism, but insufficient to reduce cumulative corridor-wide pressures
High economic efficiency due to low implementation costs and no major disruption e.g. to tourism demand, shipping routes, planning risks for fisheries remains
Slight equity improvements through shared practices, but stronger regions and well-organized sectors benefit more than smaller actors
High, as measures remain voluntary and do not impose binding constraints on fisheries, shipping, or tourism sectors
High feasibility, low additional costs, mainly administrative coordination and stakeholder engagement
Clear ecological gains from coordinated fisheries management, harmonized tourism standards, and improved protection of migratory routes
Moderate, higher costs (management, re-routing, etc.) need to be offset by better alignment between operator capacity and ecological limits

More balanced distribution of costs and benefits across regions and stakeholder groups - if safeguards/transition support are built in; otherwise, adjustment burdens can concentrate. Small-scale fisheries and nature tourism benefit from healthier ecosystems, though adjustment costs likely arise for some operators.

Medium: requires political agreement among regional authorities and acceptance of clear rules, e.g. by fisheries and tourism operators, requires sustained stakeholder engagement and mitigation/transition narrative
Moderate feasibility requires dedicated funding for coordination, monitoring, and stakeholder support, but costs are shared across regions
High effectiveness: fisheries effort, maritime traffic and tourism pressures are managed coherently across the corridor, maximizing ecosystem connectivity
High long-term efficiency based on long-term ecological improvements, but short-term adjustment costs for fisheries, shipping and some types of tourism may be significant
High equity potential if redistribution and compensation mechanisms are included; otherwise risks disproportionate impacts on small islands or specific sectors

Lower to medium, it requires binding agreements, shared governance structures, and strong political alignment, requires strong legitimacy, coalition-building, benefit-sharing mechanisms and transition support, benefits need to be locally visible

Challenging, high costs for monitoring, enforcement, coordination, requires substantial and sustained financing, potentially including new EU or transnational funding instruments, potentially including compensation or transition support for affected sectors

verify_phrases: may resist if perceived as unequal
cells.text: Requires states to give up unilateral control; unlikely without clear gains for all; Iceland and Greenland may resist if perceived as unequal outcomes.
Reflects current state; bilateral deals (e.g., UK–Faroes) persist; lacks system-wide enforcement, but politically more palatable.
Politically easy to maintain; avoids difficult compromises; risks overfishing and continued certification loss.

revenue.data_quality_note: D5.2 publishes these values, but they are inconsistent with its stated scenario assumptions and with the Annex 6 multipliers (audit A§3.1, partner question 2). They are stored verbatim and never recomputed.

countries.note: Faroese retail midpoints were used for herring and blue whiting as proxies (Table 4 note).
Tables 6-7 are positionally garbled in the PDF text layer; values are verified by presence in the table's lines only.

tuscan.note: D5.2 chapter 4 is a valuation and benefit-transfer chapter with no scenario set (L2784-2793); use the valuation calculator (WS-5).
